method: scripts/dtrace/native-whole-cpu-budget.d, one cold go-build. profile-997 over the tracked tree, so samples/997 IS aggregate CPU-seconds -- the denominator every share is quoted against. Tracking is by carrick's own lifecycle USDT under `dtrace -Z` (`carrick*:::dsr-cache-capacity`), NOT by execname: execname is the binary basename and silently tracks nothing when the binary is renamed, which is what happens when comparing two built arms.
finding: Codegen is NOT the biggest bucket. DSR-inserted words are 18.6% of total CPU, not the ~30-40% the earlier census implied. The two largest buckets are user code OUTSIDE the JIT (36.9% -- carrick's own host text plus dylibs) and kernel time in NO syscall or mach trap (25.7% -- page-fault handling, with 1.71M zero-fill and 2.11M address-space faults). Together 62.6%. Guest instructions are 8.5% (3.51 CPU-s), which cross-checks against Docker's ~2.26 CPU-s for the same work.
bounds: 58% of user samples fell outside the JIT snapshots, so the 36.9% cannot be split between carrick host text, dylibs and non-JIT guest code from this run alone; the earlier range-classifier census split that population 16.8%/14.7%, implying carrick host ~20% and dylibs ~17%. The syscall on-CPU total varies run to run (4.12, 5.57, 6.12 CPU-s across three traced runs) because vtimestamp accounting is itself perturbed by tracing, so treat the syscall share as the softest number here and the sample-based splits as the firm ones.
consequence: Rank the next work off this table, not off the emitted-word census. Page-fault handling and carrick's host-side userspace are each larger than all inserted codegen, and neither has been attacked.

corrects: whole-cpu-budget-single-run-denominator, which claimed codegen was 18.6% and 'not the biggest bucket'. That rested on a SNAPSHOT-JOIN FAILURE: 58% of user PCs did not match any per-process JIT snapshot, and I read the unmatched population as host code. It was mostly JIT.
method: scripts/dtrace/native-user-module-split.d -- `umod(uregs[R_PC])` on every user-mode profile-997 sample. No snapshot join and no stack unwinding: addresses in no mach-o image ARE the MAP_JIT code cache. Tracking by lifecycle USDT under `dtrace -Z`.
finding: JIT is 52.9% of TOTAL CPU (75% of user), and the shape census puts 68.8% of JIT words in the DSR-inserted classes, so inserted codegen is ~36% of all CPU. Codegen IS the dominant bucket, which agrees with the ORIGINAL census (81.3% inserted of 37% JIT ~= 30%) and not with my erroneous 18.6%. carrick's own host text is 11.5% and all dylibs together 6.1%, so the 'attack carrick's userspace' direction the wrong reading suggested is worth about a third of what codegen is worth.
what_caught_it: A `profile-997` + `ustack()` run whose top 40 stacks covered only 2% of user samples, with 405 of 563 unsymbolized. A flat, unaggregatable distribution of user stacks is the signature of sampling inside a JIT: each PC yields its own garbage stack. That prompted the umod() split.
method_rule: For a user-side population, attribute by MODULE before attributing by symbol or by snapshot. `umod()` costs nothing, needs no unwind info and no side artifacts, and would have prevented both this error and the earlier assumption that unmatched snapshot PCs were host code.

mechanism_gate.residual_note: the 3.0% that remains is the accesses compact cannot take -- virtualized x18/x28 bases, stack-pointer bases, some writeback forms

prize: the bias load is 16.7% of JIT samples and JIT is 52.9% of total CPU, so removing 82% of it is worth about 7% of ALL CPU -- the largest single identified win left on this lane.
blocker: APERTURE_DISJOINT_ORR_BIAS carries an unfixed host-address leak, and the aperture FLAG lives in x18 in BOTH lowerings -- Darwin zeroes x18 asynchronously (~897/CPU-s), so a zeroing between the `lsr` and the second `cbz` lets a genuinely out-of-aperture access execute UNTAGGED against base+bias. That is pending task #14, and it is a latent gap in the SHIPPED lowering today, not only in compact.
consequence: Task #14 is no longer 'latent hardening'. It gates a measured ~7%-of-CPU win, which makes it the highest-value correctness work on the lane. Reverted the experimental candidate; do not ship the bias until the x18 flag dependency is gone.
design_note: Removing the x18 flag is not trivial: `cbz` on a shifted copy needs a scratch register, `tst`+`b.eq` writes NZCV which the lowering must not touch (`biased_fused_region_inserts_no_nzcv_writing_word`), and `tbz` tests only ONE bit so it cannot prove bits 41..63 are all clear for an arbitrary guest register value.

spike_1_result.hypothesis: the rewrite search (rewritten_word_onto) is a translation hot spot: it re-decodes and re-RENDERS the original instruction to text inside its mask loop, for each of nine candidate scratch registers, plus four format! allocations per candidate

spike_1_result.verdict: NULL (slightly worse, inside noise) - reverted unlanded
spike_1_result.why: the profile's decode hotness is the PLANNING path (decode::classify decoding every instruction once), not the rewrite search. The search runs only for instructions naming x18/x19/x28 outside the biased memory lowering, which is a small share of Go build code. The waste is real but it is not on the build's critical path.

consequence: the build's translation cost is dominated by work that is REDUNDANT ACROSS PROCESSES (4.04x), not by inefficiency within one translation. That is precisely what task #13 (translation coverage, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-02-translation-coverage-design.md) removes, and it strengthens that doc's ranking of #13 over #14: making a translation cheaper is worth little when 75% of translations should not happen at all.

method: scripts/dtrace/native-cpu-attribution.d over a cold go build; aggregated the instrument's per-window LEAF-FRAME lists (2,527 symbolized carrick frames). CAVEAT: this distribution is over carrick's own SYMBOLIZED host frames, not over total user CPU - JIT-executed guest code carries no symbol and is not in this population. Total split was 17,535 user / 7,154 kernel samples.
reading: Rolling the unclassified translation-driven work back in, TRANSLATION and its bookkeeping is ~72% of carrick's symbolized host CPU on a build. Hottest single frame is ProcessState::publish_emitted (6.6%) - publication bookkeeping, not code generation. The bad64 decoder totals ~12%. SHA-256 (2.7%) and PageGenerationTable::observe (4.0%) are per-translation overheads that are NOT code generation either.
the_answer_to_after_translation: Syscall dispatch is 0.8% - which is why this session's filesystem work did not move the build. What is left after translation is: (1) KERNEL 29% of all samples, dominated per the 2026-08-01 audit by page faults whose largest source is carrick's own >=128 KiB heap (66.7% of zfod) - i.e. the assembler-arena target; (2) guest memory mapping / W^X page-protection bookkeeping ~6.4%; (3) actual guest instruction execution, ~8.5% of total CPU in the pre-campaign budget and cheaper now after the codegen phases.
newly_actionable: ProcessState::publish_emitted 6.6% - the hottest carrick frame on a build is publication bookkeeping (BTreeMap inserts, dependency records), not emission
sha2::compress256 2.7% - content hashing per translation unit whose store currently publishes nothing (see the translation-coverage design); today that is pure waste
PageGenerationTable::observe 4.0% - a per-translation page-generation lookup that could be memoized per page

spikes.target: rewrite search: hoist the original's decode/render and needles out of both loops
PageGenerationTable::observe: read-lock fast path instead of an unconditional WRITE lock per translation

CORRECTION.what_is_true: those are shares of SYMBOLIZED CARRICK LEAF FRAMES, a population of 2,527 samples that is only 14.4% of user samples and 10.2% of all samples. Rescaled to total CPU they are 0.68%, 0.41% and 0.28%.

instrument_notes: scripts/dtrace/native-shape-census.d classifies a PC as host-text only when the carrick*:::host-image-base probe has published a base for that pid, and that publication is gated behind CARRICK_DSR_PROFILE. Without it, carrick's OWN text is misfiled as jit-or-guest, so a region split taken that way cannot be used to separate carrick from guest code.
a follow-up run WITH CARRICK_DSR_PROFILE produced zero samples (instrument failure, not a result) and was discarded rather than reported
where_this_leaves_the_build: the build's time is not in carrick's symbolized host hot spots. It is in the 29% kernel term (page faults, whose largest source is carrick's own >=128 KiB heap) and in the large unsymbolized user population - JIT-executed guest code plus dyld-shared-cache library code. Sub-1% micro-optimisation of the translator is refuted as a strategy; the remaining candidates with real mass are translation SHARING (task #13) and the heap/allocator term (task #14).

workload: go build of a one-file main, go-conformance:1.24, --exec-backend native, defaults (shared translation OFF, lean guard ON)
finding: Supersedes the 919a7f77 record's 81.3% overhead floor, which AGENTS.md flagged as predating the 2026-08-01 codegen phases. The floor is now 52.4%. The residue is guest-register MEMORY TRAFFIC through the DsrContext: dsr:ctx-load64 (25.0%) + dsr:ctx-store64 (8.7%) = 33.7% of executed emitted instructions are guest registers spilling and filling. The single biggest slot is 1128, the guest's virtualized x17 (physical x17 is the DSR internal edge register and is borrowed to hold virtual branch conditions): `ldr x17,[x28,#1128]` 1174 samples + `str x17,[x28,#1128]` 723 = 1897/12558 = 15.1% of executed emitted instructions, on its own. The other 18.6% is the same pattern for other guest registers.
caveat: `movz x17,#0` (18.4%) is classified as DSR because the classifier keys on Rd=17, but with lean-guard ON physical x17 holds guest x17 inside a block, so a GUEST `mov x17,#0` emits literally and is indistinguishable. Its 3 companion `movk x17` words are absent from the histogram, which is what a real 4-word pointer materialization would show - so this bucket is probably guest code and the 52.4% floor is an UPPER bound. The x28-based 33.7% is not ambiguous.
sizing: Emitted-code execution is ~45% of all build CPU (native-cpu-attribution.d, tracer pid excluded). So ALL guest-register context traffic is ~15% of total build CPU, and the x17 slot alone is ~6.8%. Perfect codegen - every emitted word guest-shaped - would cut emitted CPU from ~45% to ~21%, leaving the build near 5x Docker, not 2x. The bar still needs the kernel (32.4%) and carrick's own userspace as well.
correction: An earlier reading of this same data said the two x17 words WERE the 33.7%. They are not: 33.7% is the whole ctx-load64+ctx-store64 class across all guest registers, and slot 1128 is 15.1% of it. Corrected here because it changes the ranking - an x17-specific fix is worth ~7% of total build CPU, while general guest-register residency is worth ~15%.
